name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
title: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
answer: Combining qualitative and quantitative data, often called mixed methods, is the practice of bringing narrative, observational, or interview material together with counts, measurements, or statistical summaries in one study. It sits in qualitative analysis and mixed methods, and it is used when a question needs both depth and breadth, such as understanding why a pattern appears and how widely it holds. The scope includes design choices about sequence, priority, and the point of integration, not just the mechanical joining of two datasets. It also covers the interpretation of divergence, where the two strands tell different stories.

sections.body: Combining qualitative and quantitative data, often called mixed methods, is the practice of bringing narrative, observational, or interview material together with counts, measurements, or statistical summaries in one study. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on data collection and analysis tools that can handle text, audio, video, and structured tables. Qualitative coding software such as NVivo or MAXQDA supports annotation and theme building, while statistical environments such as R, Python, or SPSS handle quantitative analysis. A shared data model, consistent identifiers, and a secure repository are needed so that records can be linked without losing context. Transcription services, survey platforms, and version control also form part of the practical stack.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Researchers typically choose a mixed methods design, such as explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, or convergent parallel, and then define how the strands will connect. Qualitative data may be coded into themes, while quantitative data may be cleaned and modeled, and the integration can happen through joint displays, meta matrices, or transformation of one data type into the other. Analysts often use triangulation to compare findings, and they document decision points so that another researcher can follow the path. The method is iterative, because early quantitative results can reshape interview questions and early qualitative findings can suggest new variables.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Combining data types raises consent, privacy, and reidentification risks, especially when quotes or small groups are linked to survey responses. Provenance matters because each strand has its own collection history, sampling logic, and missing data pattern, and those details must be recorded. Researchers need clear permissions for secondary use, secure storage, and rules for deidentification before integration. On this site, content links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which supports traceability to the source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more transparent integration, with reporting standards that require authors to state exactly where and how qualitative and quantitative findings were combined. Machine learning and natural language processing are being used to assist coding and to scale text analysis, but human judgment remains central to interpretation. There is growing interest in participatory and community based mixed methods that give participants a role in shaping both the questions and the measures. As more studies publish their data and code, replication and secondary analysis of mixed methods work should become more feasible.
